title: Neurosyphilis with dementia and bilateral hippocampal atrophy on brain magnetic resonance imaging
case_prompt:
A 33-year-old Bulgarian man was evaluated for an 18-month history of progressive attention and memory impairment, apathy, anxiety, and irritability. His brother first noted confusion and forgetfulness that interfered with his work as a construction worker. The patient had limited formal education but had been fully independent in activities of daily living until symptom onset.

On examination, he was not fully oriented to time but was relatively oriented to place. Neuropsychological testing showed mild to moderate dementia (MMSE score 16/30), severe verbal learning impairment (immediate recall 4/10 words; delayed recall 1/10; recognition 0/10), difficulty recalling personal information, mild anomia, poor categorical fluency (10 animals/min), and a severe dysexecutive syndrome (coding score 8 with two mistakes; letter fluency 1 “M”-word/min). 

Neurological examination revealed preserved pupillary light and accommodation reflexes without signs of Argyll-Robertson pupils, but pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs, dysarthria, and impaired coordination were present. Routine blood tests (CBC, electrolytes, glucose, liver and renal function, thyroid function, B12, folate) were normal.

Cerebrospinal fluid was clear, with 1×10^6/L erythrocytes, 39×10^6/L leukocytes (82% lymphocytes), protein 0.88 g/L, and positive oligoclonal bands. Serum VDRL titer was 1:128 and TPHA 1:2560; CSF VDRL was 1:64 and TPHA 1:640. HIV testing was negative.

MRI of the brain demonstrated moderate cortical atrophy and marked bilateral hippocampal atrophy on FLAIR and T1-weighted images, without focal areas of increased signal intensity.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Early onset Alzheimer’s disease was considered because “the cognitive and behavioral symptoms, neuropsychological profile, MRI data, and the early age at onset, were compatible with a diagnosis of probable EOAD.”  
2. Herpes simplex encephalitis was in the differential due to mesiotemporal involvement, but imaging lacked typical findings: “there are no areas of increased signal intensity in the FLAIR and T2W images.”  
3. Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis was considered given medial temporal lobe abnormalities, but the subacute–chronic course and absence of T2 hyperintensities argued against it: “temporal lobe imaging abnormalities … include … paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis,” yet the imaging did not show hyperintense lesions.  
4. Neurosyphilis was confirmed by serologic and CSF tests: “diagnosis of active neurosyphilis was based on positive results of the Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test/ Treponema pallidum hemaglutination assay … in blood and CSF samples.”
